title: How Fleas Work
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about I Heart New York merchandise and a news story that oriental rat fleas carrying the plague bacterium were found on New York rats. They then cover fleas as ectoparasites: about 2,000 species, the cat flea and dog flea, their smooth bodies with sclerites, backward-pointing hairs that let them slip through fur, and mouthparts for blood meals. Next is the flea life cycle (smooth eggs, about 12 days to hatch at about 70 F and humidity, three larval instars, pupal cocoon that waits for host signals), flea larvae eating debris and tapeworm eggs, and diseases fleas spread (tapeworm, murine typhus, plague, flea-bite reactions). They discuss the nineteenth-century flea circus and fleas' strength in pulling carts, Albert Tolato, and a personal infestation story. Control advice follows (finding the source, vacuuming, washing, nematodes, insect growth regulators, and home remedies that don't work). The episode covers sand fleas (chigoe / jigger, tungiasis) in Africa and the Caribbean, and ends with a listener mail segment correcting film facts from Travis Dukelo about Birdman, Hitchcock, and film noir.

segments.title: Opening banter and New York rat plague news
segments.summary: Hosts joke about I Heart New York shirts and the store, then discuss a news story that plague-carrying oriental rat fleas were found on New York rats, while the bacterium itself was not found in them.

segments.title: Flea basics: hosts, parasites and blood meals
segments.summary: Fleas are ectoparasites that drink blood; there are about 2,000 species, mainly the cat flea and dog flea. The hosts note that squirrel fleas differ from pet fleas and warn against staging dead animals. Fleas take blood meals and are one-way parasites.

segments.title: Flea anatomy, jumping and grooming
segments.summary: Fleas are wingless with sclerites that protect them from squishing. They can jump about seven inches vertically and up to about 13 inches horizontally. Backward-pointing hairs let them slip through fur, and fine-tooth combs catch them. Flea dirt indicates infestation.

segments.title: Flea mouthparts and feeding
segments.summary: Flea mouthparts include lacinia that puncture skin and form a saliva channel, and a stylet with an epipharynx that sucks blood. The hosts note the suction needed for feeding.

segments.title: Flea life cycle
segments.summary: Flea eggs are smooth and fall off hosts into carpets, cracks and soil. Eggs hatch in about 12 days at around 70 F and high humidity. Larvae go through three instars, spin cocoons, and pupae can wait up to a year for host signals. Only about five percent reach adulthood, and females need blood meals to lay eggs.

segments.title: Flea diseases: tapeworms, typhus, plague and bites
segments.summary: Flea larvae eat debris and tapeworm eggs, so adults can carry tapeworms, mainly dog fleas. Flea saliva causes bite reactions, and scratching can open skin to infection. Murine typhus is spread through flea feces, and the plague bacterium can infect the flea's midgut and be regurgitated into a bite.

segments.title: Flea circuses and the strength of fleas
segments.summary: Fleas can lift up to 60 times their body weight. In the 1500s and 1600s, watchmakers such as Mark Scalliot attached tiny chains to fleas and pulled miniature carts. Trainers reportedly kept fleas in jars and harnessed them. Flea circuses appeared at Oktoberfest, Coney Island, Blackpool and elsewhere, and Albert Tolato was a noted flea circus figure.

segments.title: Flea control and infestation stories
segments.summary: The hosts share personal infestation stories and find a dead squirrel as source. They discuss control steps, including washing bedding, vacuuming, treating pets and the environment, nematodes, insect growth regulators, and home remedies that do not work.

segments.title: Sand fleas and tungiasis
segments.summary: Sand fleas, also called chigoes, jiggers or niguas, were spread to sub-Saharan Africa through the slave trade. They burrow under the skin and cause painful disability, especially in poor areas. A PhD student named Marlene studied a burrowed female that lived for two months without laying eggs, and a theory is that females can wait for males to fertilize eggs.

segments.title: Autobiography of a Flea
segments.summary: The hosts mention the nineteenth-century erotica novel Autobiography of a Flea, a London book about a flea that follows a girl.

segments.title: Listener mail: film corrections
segments.summary: Travis Dukelo writes to correct the hosts' film statements, covering Birdman's ending, the Guillermo del Toro film mix-up, James Cameron, Anatomy of a Murder versus Dial M for Murder, and the origins of surreal cinema and film noir.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite corrections and mention ways to contact the show, then sign off.
